title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 122 (Applicability to One Person Company)

content.overview: Section 122 modifies general-meeting requirements for a One Person Company and provides a written minute-book mechanism for specified business.
content.glance: The listed general-meeting provisions do not apply to an OPC as stated in section 122; the sole member records and signs decisions in the minute book as required.
content.study:
## Excluded general-meeting provisions

Section 122(1) provides that sections 98 and 100 to 111 do not apply to a One Person Company (OPC). Read the exact statutory list rather than assuming that every meeting-related provision is excluded.

## Recording the sole member's decision

Under section 122, business that would otherwise be transacted at a general meeting or by postal ballot may, in the circumstances specified by the section, be dealt with by the member communicating the resolution to the company. The resolution must be entered in the minute book and signed and dated by the member; the date of signature is treated as the date of the meeting for this purpose. The section also addresses companies required to have only one director in its specified context.

## Practical checklist

Confirm that the company qualifies as an OPC or falls within the relevant single-director provision; identify the business and any other statutory requirement; communicate the resolution to the company; enter it in the correct minute book; obtain the member's signature and date; and preserve the record.

## Limits

The OPC simplification does not remove every obligation under the Companies Act. Apply provisions not excluded by section 122 and the applicable rules to the company and transaction.

sections.title: Other obligations

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How does section 122 modify general-meeting requirements for an OPC?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Section 122(1) states that sections 98 and 100 to 111 do not apply to an OPC. In the circumstances specified in section 122, business may be transacted by the member communicating the resolution to the company and entering it in the minute book, signed and dated by the member. The signature date is treated as the meeting date for this purpose. Other statutory obligations remain unless expressly displaced.

examTips: Quote the precise sections excluded by section 122(1).
Explain the communication, minute-book entry, signature and date requirements.
revisionPoints: Section 122 contains specified OPC exceptions to general-meeting provisions.
Sole-member decisions must be recorded and signed/dated as required.
Other statutory obligations continue unless expressly excluded.

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 122 (Applicability to One Person Company). The provisions on general meetings do not apply to a one person company, which records resolutions in the minutes signed by the member. The section applies only to the persons, companies, and transactions it names. A filing, approval, or penalty arises only where the section or a rule under it says so. It does not create a power that is reserved to another section or to the Tribunal. Not a verified closure.
